title: What is Software Engineering?
explanation: Software engineering is building software that works, on time, and can be maintained. It's not just coding - it's planning, designing, testing, and working with teams. It turns ideas into reliable products.
analogy: If coding is laying bricks, software engineering is architecture - planning the building, ensuring it's safe, and making it beautiful and functional.
example: Building an app isn't just writing code. You need to plan features, design the structure, write tests, fix bugs, deploy updates, and work with others.
why_it_matters: Good engineering practices let you build complex software that doesn't collapse under its own weight. Bad practices create unmaintainable messes.
checkpoint_question: Why isn't 'just coding' enough for real software projects?
expected_answer: Code needs to be readable, maintainable, tested, and able to evolve. Without planning and practices, code becomes messy, buggy, and impossible to change without breaking things.
common_mistake: Jumping straight into coding without understanding the problem. Planning saves more time than it costs.
key_insight: Most of a software's lifetime is spent on maintenance, not initial development. Write code for the future maintainer (often yourself!).

title: Git: Tracking Your Changes
explanation: Git saves snapshots of your code (commits). You can go back to any previous version, work on experiments without breaking things, and merge work from multiple people. It's like unlimited undo for your entire project.
analogy: Git is like Google Docs version history for code - you can see every change, who made it, when, and go back to any version.
example: You try a risky change. It breaks everything. With Git, you just revert to the last working version. Without Git, you're stuck.
why_it_matters: Every professional developer uses Git. It prevents disasters, enables collaboration, and is essential for any serious project.
checkpoint_question: What is a 'commit' in Git?
expected_answer: A commit is a saved snapshot of your code at a point in time. It includes what changed and a message describing why. You can always go back to any commit.
common_mistake: Not committing often enough. Small, frequent commits make it easy to undo specific changes. Big commits are hard to undo.
code:
# Common Git commands
git init            # Start tracking a project
git add .           # Stage changes
git commit -m "Add login feature"
git log             # See history
git checkout abc123 # Go to old version
git push            # Upload to GitHub
key_insight: Write good commit messages. 'Fixed bug' is useless. 'Fix login crash when password is empty' tells the future what happened.

title: Branches: Parallel Universes
explanation: A branch is a separate line of development. You can work on a new feature without affecting the main code. When it's ready, merge it back. Multiple people can work on different branches simultaneously.
analogy: Like a 'save as' copy where you try changes. If they work, copy them back. If they fail, delete the copy. Main version stays safe.
example: Main branch is stable. Create 'add-search-feature' branch, work on search. Meanwhile, teammate works on 'fix-login-bug' branch. Both merge back when ready.
why_it_matters: Branches enable teamwork and experimentation. You can try risky changes safely, review code before merging, and work in parallel.
checkpoint_question: Why work on a branch instead of directly on the main code?
expected_answer: To keep main stable while you work. Half-finished features break things. Branches let you develop until ready, then merge when complete and tested.
common_mistake: Working on huge changes for weeks without merging. Merge often to avoid painful conflicts.
code:
# Create and switch to new branch
git checkout -b add-search-feature

# Work and commit on branch...
git commit -m "Add search UI"
git commit -m "Connect to search API"

# Switch back to main, merge branch
git checkout main
git merge add-search-feature
key_insight: Pull requests (GitHub) or merge requests (GitLab) let others review your branch before merging. This catches bugs and shares knowledge.

title: Why Write Tests?
explanation: Tests are code that checks if your code works. They run automatically and tell you if something breaks. Without tests, you don't know if changes broke existing features until users complain.
analogy: Tests are like a checklist a pilot runs before takeoff. Check engine, check wings, check fuel. Automated checks catch problems before they become disasters.
example: You add a feature and accidentally break login. Without tests: users complain. With tests: test suite immediately shows 'login test failed'.
why_it_matters: Tests give you confidence to change code. Without them, you're afraid to touch anything because you might break it.
checkpoint_question: When should you write tests?
expected_answer: Before you write the feature (Test-Driven Development) or right after. Write them early while the logic is fresh. Skipping tests creates technical debt that compounds over time.
common_mistake: Thinking tests are a waste of time. They save time by catching bugs early and making changes safe.
code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

# Test for the add function
def test_add():
    assert add(2, 3) == 5
    assert add(-1, 1) == 0
    assert add(0, 0) == 0

# Run tests
test_add()
print("All tests passed!")
key_insight: Unit tests check individual functions. Integration tests check multiple parts working together. End-to-end tests check the whole system.

title: Test-Driven Development (TDD)
explanation: TDD means writing the test before writing the code. 1) Write a failing test for what you want. 2) Write just enough code to pass the test. 3) Clean up the code. It sounds backwards but leads to better design.
analogy: Like writing the exam before studying. You know exactly what you need to learn and can focus on that.
example: Want to add 'calculate tax' function. First write test: assert calculate_tax(100) == 10. Test fails (function doesn't exist). Now write function to make it pass.
why_it_matters: TDD forces you to think about what the code should do before how to do it. It produces testable, focused code by design.
checkpoint_question: Why write the test before the code?
expected_answer: It forces you to clarify requirements (what exactly should this do?). You get instant feedback when done. The code is testable by design. You never skip writing tests.
common_mistake: Writing tests that are too specific to implementation. Test behavior (what it does), not internals (how it does it).
code:
# TDD cycle:

# 1. Write failing test
def test_calculate_tax():
    assert calculate_tax(100) == 10  # Fails - no function!

# 2. Write minimal code to pass
def calculate_tax(amount):
    return amount * 0.1  # Now test passes!

# 3. Refactor if needed
# (Clean up code while keeping tests green)
key_insight: Red-Green-Refactor: start with a failing test (red), make it pass (green), then clean up (refactor). Repeat.

title: Writing Clean Code
explanation: Clean code is readable, simple, and easy to change. Use meaningful names, keep functions short and focused, don't repeat yourself (DRY). Code is read far more than written - optimize for the reader.
analogy: Clean code is like a well-organized kitchen. Everything has a place, labeled clearly. You can find anything quickly and cook efficiently.
example: Bad: 'x = d * 0.1'. Good: 'tax = price * TAX_RATE'. The second is instantly understandable.
why_it_matters: You'll spend most time reading and modifying existing code. Clean code makes this easier and less error-prone.
checkpoint_question: Why are good variable names important?
expected_answer: Names explain what data represents. 'x' means nothing - you have to trace through code to understand. 'user_age' is instantly clear. Good names reduce the need for comments.
common_mistake: Clever code that's hard to understand. Simple, obvious code is better. You'll thank yourself later.
code:
# Bad: What does this do?
def f(l):
    return [x for x in l if x > 0]

# Good: Clear names explain intent
def get_positive_numbers(numbers):
    return [n for n in numbers if n > 0]

# Even better: Python has this built in
positive = list(filter(lambda n: n > 0, numbers))
key_insight: Functions should do one thing. If you need 'and' to describe it ('validate and save user'), split it into two functions.

title: Finding and Fixing Bugs
explanation: Bugs are mistakes that make code behave wrong. Debugging is finding the cause and fixing it. The key is systematic investigation: reproduce the bug, narrow down where it happens, understand why, fix it, and test.
analogy: Debugging is detective work. Gather clues (error messages, logs), form theories, test them, and find the culprit.
example: App crashes when saving. Where? Add print statements to trace the path. Crashes after 'loading user'. Check that code. Found: user can be null.
why_it_matters: All programmers debug constantly. Getting good at it saves hours of frustration and makes you effective.
checkpoint_question: What's the first step when you find a bug?
expected_answer: Reproduce it reliably. If you can't reproduce it, you can't fix it or verify the fix. Figure out exactly what steps cause the bug.
common_mistake: Changing random things hoping to fix it. This often introduces new bugs. Understand the cause first.
code:
# Debugging with print statements
def calculate_total(items):
    print(f"Items received: {items}")  # What did we get?
    total = 0
    for item in items:
        print(f"Processing: {item}")  # Each step
        total += item.price
        print(f"Running total: {total}")
    return total

# Now you can see exactly where things go wrong
key_insight: Rubber duck debugging: explain the problem out loud (or to a rubber duck). Often you'll realize the answer while explaining.

title: Working with Others
explanation: Real software is built by teams. This requires communication, code reviews, shared standards, and coordination. The code must be readable by others, and everyone must stay aligned on what they're building.
analogy: Like a band - each musician is skilled, but they need to play together, follow the same tempo, and communicate or it sounds terrible.
example: You write a feature. Teammate reviews it, catches a bug you missed, suggests a cleaner approach. Code improves, knowledge spreads.
why_it_matters: Almost all professional software is built in teams. Collaboration skills are as important as coding skills.
checkpoint_question: Why do code reviews even when the code works?
expected_answer: To catch bugs before production. To share knowledge (others learn the code). To maintain consistency. To get fresh perspectives. Working code can still be improved.
common_mistake: Taking code review comments personally. They're about the code, not you. Everyone's code can be improved.
key_insight: Documentation, clear commit messages, and readable code are how you communicate with future teammates (including future you).

title: Getting Code to Users
explanation: Deployment is getting your code running for real users. This includes building, testing, releasing to servers, and monitoring. Automated pipelines (CI/CD) run tests and deploy automatically when code changes.
analogy: Like a book's journey from author to reader: editing (tests), printing (building), shipping (deploying), and checking store shelves (monitoring).
example: You merge code to main branch. Pipeline runs tests automatically. Tests pass → code is deployed to production. Users see the update within minutes.
why_it_matters: Fast, safe deployment lets you ship features and fixes quickly. Manual deployment is slow and error-prone.
checkpoint_question: Why automate deployment instead of doing it manually?
expected_answer: Automation is consistent - no missed steps. It's fast and repeatable. It catches errors before production. Manual deployments are slow and humans make mistakes.
common_mistake: Deploying on Fridays. If something breaks, you spend your weekend fixing it. Deploy early in the week when you can respond.
code:
# Example CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions)
name: Deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  test-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - name: Run tests
        run: python -m pytest
      - name: Deploy if tests pass
        run: ./deploy.sh
key_insight: Deploy small changes frequently rather than big changes rarely. Small changes are easier to debug when something goes wrong.

title: Growing as a Developer
explanation: Software engineering skills develop over years. Start by building things - real projects teach more than tutorials. Read code, contribute to open source, learn from others, and keep up with changes in the field.
analogy: Like learning an instrument: lessons (tutorials) start you off, but playing real music (building projects) develops true skill.
example: Build a project that solves your own problem. You'll encounter real challenges: debugging, design decisions, deployment. This builds practical skills.
why_it_matters: The field evolves constantly. Lifelong learning isn't optional. The best engineers are always growing.
checkpoint_question: What's more valuable: learning many languages or mastering one deeply?
expected_answer: Master one deeply first. Fundamentals transfer between languages. Deep knowledge makes learning others easier. Broad-but-shallow knowledge means you can't actually build anything well.
common_mistake: Tutorial hell - watching tutorials without building. You learn by doing, not watching.
key_insight: The best way to learn is to build something you actually want to use. Motivation sustains you through hard parts.

title: Technical Debt: Cutting Corners
explanation: Technical debt is taking shortcuts now that create more work later. Like financial debt: quick now, but you pay interest. Some debt is strategic (ship faster), but too much debt slows everything down.
analogy: Like a messy room. Quick to drop clothes on the floor, but eventually you spend more time searching than you saved by not organizing.
example: Copy-paste code to ship fast. Now there are 5 copies. A bug fix needs 5 changes. Forget one? Bug persists. The debt compounds.
why_it_matters: All projects accumulate debt. Recognizing it helps you decide when to pay it down and when to accept it strategically.
checkpoint_question: When might technical debt be a good tradeoff?
expected_answer: When speed matters more than perfection: testing an idea, meeting a critical deadline, proving a concept. The key is knowing you'll pay it back, not pretending it doesn't exist.
common_mistake: Never paying down debt. Eventually velocity drops to near-zero because everything is tangled and fragile.
key_insight: Refactoring is paying down debt. Regularly allocate time for cleanup, or debt accumulates until it's overwhelming.

title: Abstraction: Hiding Complexity
explanation: Abstraction hides complicated details behind simple interfaces. You use a function without knowing how it works. You drive a car without understanding the engine. Good abstractions make complex systems usable.
analogy: A light switch abstracts electricity. You don't need to understand circuits - flip switch, get light. The complexity is hidden.
example: list.sort() sorts a list. You don't know which algorithm it uses. You don't care. The abstraction gives you a simple interface to complex logic.
why_it_matters: Abstraction is how we manage complexity. Without it, every programmer would need to understand every detail of every system.
checkpoint_question: What makes a good abstraction?
expected_answer: It hides details you don't need while exposing controls you do. It's stable - the interface doesn't change even if implementation does. It's predictable - does what the name suggests.
common_mistake: Leaky abstractions - when details leak through. Like when you need to know database internals to use an 'easy' database library.
code:
# Abstraction: you don't know HOW it works
result = database.find_user(email)
# vs. writing SQL, handling connections, parsing results...

# Good abstraction: simple interface
file.save(data)  # Don't care if it's SSD, cloud, etc.

# Leaky abstraction: details leak through
# "Easy" image library that requires knowing pixel formats
key_insight: All abstractions leak somewhat. The best ones leak rarely, in predictable places, with good documentation.

title: Agile: Adapting to Change
explanation: Agile is a development approach emphasizing short cycles, frequent delivery, and adapting to change. Instead of planning everything upfront, you build a little, get feedback, adjust, repeat. Embrace change rather than fight it.
analogy: Like GPS navigation that recalculates when you take a wrong turn, vs a paper map that assumes you'll follow the exact route.
example: 2-week sprints. Each sprint: plan a few features, build them, demo to users, get feedback, adjust priorities. Repeat. Always delivering working software.
why_it_matters: Requirements change. Users don't know what they want until they see it. Agile embraces this reality instead of pretending plans are perfect.
checkpoint_question: Why deliver working software frequently instead of one big release?
expected_answer: Early feedback catches wrong assumptions before you build too much. Users see progress. Problems surface sooner when changes are smaller. You always have something working to show.
common_mistake: Doing 'agile' without the principles - just having standups while still doing big waterfall planning. The rituals aren't the point.
key_insight: The Agile Manifesto values: individuals over processes, working software over documentation, collaboration over contracts, responding to change over following a plan.

title: The Art of Code Review
explanation: Code review is having others examine your code before it merges. It catches bugs, shares knowledge, maintains standards, and improves design. Both reviewer and author learn. It's a conversation, not a judgment.
analogy: Like having an editor read your writing. They catch mistakes you're blind to and suggest improvements. The final work is better.
example: You submit code. Teammate reviews: 'This could be null here - add a check.' You fix it. Bug prevented before it reached users.
why_it_matters: Code review is one of the most effective ways to improve code quality and spread knowledge across a team.
checkpoint_question: What should code reviewers focus on?
expected_answer: Bugs and logic errors, security issues, readability, maintainability, test coverage, adherence to team standards. Not nitpicking style that linters can catch automatically.
common_mistake: Taking review comments personally. They're about the code, not you. Everyone's code can be improved.
code:
# Good code review comments focus on:

# 1. Bugs and issues
# "This could throw an exception if user is null"

# 2. Clarity
# "I'm not sure what 'process_data' does - could we name it more specifically?"

# 3. Alternatives
# "This works, but using a dictionary here might be clearer"

# 4. Questions (when unsure)
# "Why do we need this step? I might be missing context."
key_insight: Review your own code first. Step away, then read it fresh. You'll catch many issues before anyone else sees them.

title: Design Patterns: Reusable Solutions
explanation: Design patterns are proven solutions to common problems. Instead of reinventing, you apply patterns: Singleton (one instance), Factory (create objects), Observer (notify on changes). They're templates, not copy-paste code.
analogy: Like cooking techniques. 'Sautéing' is a pattern - you don't reinvent it, you learn it and apply it to many dishes.
example: Need to notify multiple objects when something changes? That's the Observer pattern. Need to create objects without specifying exact types? That's Factory.
why_it_matters: Patterns give you a vocabulary to discuss design. They're battle-tested solutions you don't have to discover yourself.
checkpoint_question: Why use patterns instead of solving problems your own way?
expected_answer: Patterns are proven and well-understood. Others recognize them immediately. They handle edge cases you might miss. They communicate intent clearly.
common_mistake: Applying patterns where they don't fit. Not every problem needs a pattern. Simple solutions are often better.
key_insight: The Gang of Four book describes 23 classic patterns. You don't need to memorize them - recognize common problems and look up solutions.

title: Monitoring: Knowing What's Happening
explanation: Monitoring tracks your running system: response times, error rates, resource usage. Without it, you don't know if things are working until users complain. Good monitoring catches problems early and helps diagnose issues.
analogy: Like a car dashboard. Without gauges, you wouldn't know you're low on fuel until you stop. Monitoring is your system's dashboard.
example: Error rate spikes from 0.1% to 5%. Alert triggers. You investigate before users notice. Turns out a new deploy broke something. You rollback.
why_it_matters: You can't fix what you can't see. Monitoring is essential for maintaining reliable systems.
checkpoint_question: What's the difference between logs and metrics?
expected_answer: Logs are detailed events ('User 123 logged in at 3:45'). Metrics are numbers over time (logins per minute, error rate). Logs help diagnose specific issues; metrics show overall health and trends.
common_mistake: Only logging errors. Log key events and successes too. 'No errors' doesn't mean 'working correctly' if there's also no activity.
code:
# Key things to monitor:

# Application metrics
# - Response times (p50, p95, p99)
# - Error rate (% of requests failing)
# - Request rate (requests per second)

# System metrics
# - CPU usage
# - Memory usage
# - Disk space

# Business metrics
# - Signups per hour
# - Orders per day
# - Revenue
key_insight: Alerting on metrics catches problems. But too many alerts cause 'alert fatigue' - people ignore them. Alert on actionable issues only.

title: Handling Failures Gracefully
explanation: Things fail: servers crash, networks hiccup, databases slow down. Good systems handle failures gracefully: retry transient errors, degrade functionality when services are down, fail fast when something is broken.
analogy: Like a building with backup generators. When main power fails, critical systems keep running. The building handles the failure gracefully.
example: Payment service is slow. Instead of timing out with an error, show 'Processing your payment...' and retry in background. User sees success when it eventually works.
why_it_matters: Users judge your system by how it handles failures, not by how it works when everything's perfect.
checkpoint_question: What is 'graceful degradation'?
expected_answer: When part of a system fails, the rest keeps working with reduced functionality. If recommendations are down, still show products (just not personalized). Better than complete failure.
common_mistake: One failure cascading to take down everything. Design systems so failures are isolated.
key_insight: Chaos engineering: intentionally break things in production to verify systems handle failures. Netflix's 'Chaos Monkey' randomly kills servers.

title: Microservices vs Monolith
explanation: A monolith is one big application. Microservices split into many small, independent services. Monoliths are simpler to start; microservices scale better but add complexity. There's no universally right choice.
analogy: Monolith: one big restaurant kitchen. Microservices: food court with specialized vendors. Food court scales better but needs more coordination.
example: Monolith: one codebase handles users, orders, payments. Microservices: separate user service, order service, payment service - each deployed independently.
why_it_matters: This is a major architectural decision. Understanding tradeoffs helps you make appropriate choices for your situation.
checkpoint_question: When might a monolith be better than microservices?
expected_answer: Small teams, new products (not sure what to build yet), simpler deployment needs. Microservices add overhead: network calls, distributed debugging, deployment complexity. Start simple, split later if needed.
common_mistake: Starting with microservices because 'that's what big companies do.' They split after hitting monolith limitations.
key_insight: A 'distributed monolith' is the worst of both: microservices that must all deploy together and share databases. If splitting, split properly.

title: Designing Good APIs
explanation: A good API is consistent, predictable, and hard to misuse. Use clear naming, consistent patterns, meaningful errors. Think about the caller's experience. A good API makes correct usage easy and incorrect usage hard.
analogy: Like a well-designed door handle. Push plates on push doors, pull handles on pull doors. Design that guides correct usage.
example: GET /users/123 returns user. POST /users creates user. DELETE /users/123 removes user. Consistent, predictable patterns.
why_it_matters: APIs are contracts. Once published, they're hard to change. Good design saves pain for everyone who uses it.
checkpoint_question: Why return proper HTTP status codes?
expected_answer: Codes communicate what happened. 200 = success, 404 = not found, 400 = bad request, 500 = server error. Callers can handle each case appropriately. Using 200 for everything forces callers to parse responses.
common_mistake: Returning 200 OK with an error message in the body. Use proper status codes so callers can handle errors without parsing.
code:
# Good API design

# Consistent URL patterns
GET /users          # List users
GET /users/123      # Get one user
POST /users         # Create user
PUT /users/123      # Update user
DELETE /users/123   # Delete user

# Proper status codes
200 OK              # Success
201 Created         # Resource created
400 Bad Request     # Invalid input
404 Not Found       # Resource doesn't exist
500 Server Error    # Something broke
key_insight: Versioning: include version in URL (/api/v1/users) or header. Lets you evolve APIs without breaking existing clients.

title: Writing Useful Documentation
explanation: Good docs explain WHY, not just WHAT. Show examples. Keep it updated. Document for your audience - beginner tutorials, API references, architecture overviews serve different needs.
analogy: Like a recipe book. Quick reference (ingredient list), step-by-step instructions (how-to), technique explanations (why this works). Different sections for different needs.
example: README: what this is, how to install, quick example. API docs: every endpoint with examples. Architecture: system overview for new team members.
why_it_matters: Code without docs is hard to use, maintain, and contribute to. Docs multiply the value of your code.
checkpoint_question: What's more important: comprehensive docs or accurate docs?
expected_answer: Accurate. Wrong documentation is worse than none - it misleads and wastes time. Keep docs updated when code changes. A small accurate doc beats a large outdated one.
common_mistake: Writing docs once and never updating. Stale docs actively mislead. Delete or update obsolete sections.
code:
# Good README structure:

# Project Name
One-sentence description of what this does.

## Quick Start
```bash
pip install myproject
myproject --help
```

## Example
```python
from myproject import main
main('example')  # Does the thing
```

## Documentation
Link to full docs.

## Contributing
How to contribute.
key_insight: The best docs are close to the code. Docstrings, comments, and type hints stay synced. Separate docs drift.

title: Feature Flags: Safe Deployment
explanation: Feature flags let you deploy code but keep features hidden. Enable for some users (testing), then gradually roll out, then enable for everyone. If problems arise, disable instantly without redeploying.
analogy: Like a light switch for features. Code is deployed but turned off. Flip the switch when ready. Flip back if something's wrong.
example: New checkout flow: deploy with flag off. Enable for 1% of users. Monitor. No problems? Enable for 10%, then 50%, then 100%. Problems? Disable immediately.
why_it_matters: Separates deploy from release. You can deploy safely and control rollout. Reduces risk and enables experimentation.
checkpoint_question: How are feature flags different from branches?
expected_answer: Branches separate code before deploy. Feature flags control behavior after deploy. You can merge code to main, deploy it, but keep it hidden. Then enable runtime, no redeploy needed.
common_mistake: Never removing old flags. They accumulate, making code confusing. Remove flags after features are fully rolled out.
key_insight: A/B testing uses feature flags. Show version A to half, version B to half, measure which performs better.

title: Integration Testing: Parts Working Together
explanation: Unit tests check individual pieces. Integration tests check that pieces work together: database connections, API calls, service interactions. They're slower but catch issues that unit tests miss.
analogy: Unit test: does each instrument work? Integration test: does the orchestra sound good together? Both are needed.
example: Unit test: does the 'calculate tax' function work? Integration test: does the checkout flow correctly calculate tax, charge the card, and send confirmation email?
why_it_matters: Real bugs often occur at boundaries between components. Integration tests catch these before users do.
checkpoint_question: Why not just have integration tests without unit tests?
expected_answer: Integration tests are slow and hard to debug. Which component failed? Unit tests are fast, pinpoint failures, and catch more edge cases. Use both: many unit tests, fewer integration tests.
common_mistake: Skipping integration tests because unit tests pass. Each component works alone but they might not work together.
code:
# Unit test: isolated function
def test_calculate_tax():
    assert calculate_tax(100) == 10

# Integration test: real database, real API
def test_checkout_flow():
    # Create test user in real test database
    user = create_test_user()
    
    # Add items to real cart
    add_to_cart(user, 'product_1')
    
    # Process real checkout flow
    result = checkout(user)
    
    # Verify database was updated
    assert Order.query.filter_by(user=user).count() == 1
key_insight: The testing pyramid: many unit tests (fast, cheap), fewer integration tests, even fewer end-to-end tests. Balance coverage with speed.

title: Working with Legacy Code
explanation: Legacy code is existing code you must work with - often poorly documented, without tests, using old patterns. You can't rewrite everything. Learn to understand it, improve it incrementally, and add tests before changes.
analogy: Like renovating an old house while living in it. You can't tear it down and rebuild. Make careful improvements without breaking what works.
example: Add tests for the area you're changing. Make small, safe changes. Refactor incrementally. Leave code better than you found it, but don't try to fix everything at once.
why_it_matters: Most real work involves existing code. Skill with legacy code is essential. It teaches you about real-world constraints.
checkpoint_question: Why add tests before changing legacy code?
expected_answer: Tests verify current behavior. Without them, you don't know if your changes broke something. Add tests that pass now, then change the code, tests catch regressions.
common_mistake: Big-bang rewrites. They take forever, introduce new bugs, and often fail. Incremental improvement is safer.
code:
# Working with legacy code strategy:

# 1. Add tests for existing behavior
def test_mysterious_function_current_behavior():
    assert mysterious_function(x) == current_output

# 2. Make small changes
# 3. Run tests after each change
# 4. Refactor incrementally

# DON'T:
# - Rewrite everything at once
# - Change without tests
# - Assume you understand old code fully
key_insight: The Strangler Fig pattern: build new functionality alongside old, gradually migrate, eventually remove old code. Safe legacy replacement.

title: Event-Driven Architecture
explanation: Instead of direct calls between components, they communicate through events. Services publish events ('order created'), other services subscribe and react. Loose coupling - publisher doesn't know or care who's listening.
analogy: Like a newspaper. Publisher prints news. Readers subscribe. Publisher doesn't know each reader. Readers don't coordinate with each other.
example: Order placed → event published. Inventory service reduces stock. Notification service sends email. Billing service charges card. Each handles the event independently.
why_it_matters: Event-driven enables loose coupling, independent scaling, and easy extension. Add new subscribers without changing publishers.
checkpoint_question: What's a downside of event-driven architecture?
expected_answer: Harder to trace flow (events go through queues, not direct calls). Eventual consistency (events process asynchronously). Debugging distributed events is complex. Ordering can be tricky.
common_mistake: Using events for everything. Simple request-response is often clearer. Events add complexity that's only worth it for loose coupling needs.
key_insight: Event sourcing goes further: store events as the source of truth, derive current state by replaying events. Full audit trail built in.

title: Continuous Integration/Delivery (CI/CD)
explanation: CI: automatically build and test code when pushed. CD: automatically deploy after tests pass. Catch bugs early, deploy frequently, reduce risk. Small changes, fast feedback, reliable releases.
analogy: Like an assembly line with quality checks at each step. Problems caught early, before they pile up. Smooth, continuous flow to production.
example: Push code → CI runs tests (5 min) → tests pass → auto-deploy to staging → manual approve → deploy to production. All automated.
why_it_matters: Manual deployment is slow and error-prone. CI/CD enables teams to deploy daily instead of monthly. Faster feedback, safer releases.
checkpoint_question: Why deploy frequently in small batches?
expected_answer: Small changes are easier to debug if something goes wrong. Less risk per deploy. Fast rollback. Continuous feedback from users. Big batch releases are scary and risky.
common_mistake: Having CI but never fixing broken builds. A broken build should be top priority. If builds are always broken, CI isn't helping.
code:
# Example CI pipeline (GitHub Actions)
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v2
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest  # Run tests
  
  deploy:
    needs: test  # Only after tests pass
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh
key_insight: The best CI/CD gives feedback in minutes. If tests take hours, developers move on and context-switch. Keep builds fast.

title: Writing Technical Specs
explanation: Before building, write what you'll build. Problem statement, proposed solution, alternatives considered, trade-offs, timeline. Gets buy-in, catches issues early, creates shared understanding.
analogy: Like architectural plans before building a house. Discover problems in planning, not construction. Align everyone on what's being built.
example: Problem: search is slow. Proposal: add caching. Alternatives: better queries, new database. Trade-offs: cache invalidation complexity vs speed gain. Decision: implement caching.
why_it_matters: Specs prevent 'I thought you meant...' disasters. They force clarity of thought. They're documentation of decisions.
checkpoint_question: Why document alternatives you didn't choose?
expected_answer: Shows you considered options. Explains why current approach. Prevents re-debating later ('why didn't you just...'). Future reader understands the context.
common_mistake: Specs that are too detailed or too vague. Hit the right level: enough for shared understanding, not a line-by-line code description.
key_insight: A spec should answer: What problem? Why now? What solution? What trade-offs? What's the rollout plan? What could go wrong?

title: Code Reviews: Learning From Each Other
explanation: Before merging code, someone else reviews it. They check for bugs, suggest improvements, and ensure it meets standards. Reviews catch issues early and spread knowledge across the team.
analogy: Like having an editor review your writing. Fresh eyes catch things you missed. You learn their perspective, they learn yours.
example: You submit a pull request. Teammate comments: 'This could be null - add a check.' You fix it before it becomes a production bug.
why_it_matters: Code reviews find bugs (cheaper to fix early), share knowledge (reduces bus factor), improve code quality, and enforce consistency.
checkpoint_question: What makes a good code review comment?
expected_answer: Specific, actionable, and kind. Says what's wrong and suggests how to fix it. Focuses on the code, not the person. Explains reasoning. Asks questions when unsure.
common_mistake: Rubber-stamping reviews ('LGTM' without reading). Reviews only work if reviewers engage. Spend time; find real issues.
key_insight: Review your own code first. Read it as if someone else wrote it. You'll catch obvious issues before wasting reviewer's time.

title: The Art of Debugging
explanation: Debugging is finding and fixing bugs. The key skill: forming hypotheses and testing them. What do I think is happening? How can I verify? Narrow down until you find the exact issue.
analogy: Like being a detective. Gather clues (logs, error messages). Form theories. Test them. Eliminate possibilities until only the culprit remains.
example: Bug: users can't log in. Check logs - auth service timing out. Check auth service - database connection failing. Check database - connection limit hit. Root cause found.
why_it_matters: Everyone writes bugs. The difference between junior and senior developers is often debugging speed. Systematic debugging is a superpower.
checkpoint_question: You have a bug but no idea where. How do you start?
expected_answer: Reproduce it reliably first. Check error logs. Binary search: is the problem in the frontend or backend? Which function? Narrow scope until you isolate the issue.
common_mistake: Changing random things hoping to fix it. Understand first, fix second. Random changes create more bugs and hide the real issue.
code:
# Debugging techniques:
# 1. Print/log statements
print(f'Got here with value: {x}')

# 2. Use a debugger - set breakpoints
import pdb; pdb.set_trace()  # Python

# 3. Check assumptions
assert user is not None, 'Expected user'

# 4. Simplify - minimal reproduction
# 5. Read the error message carefully
# 6. Check recent changes (git diff)
# 7. Rubber duck - explain the problem out loud
key_insight: The bug is almost never where you first look. If it were obvious, you wouldn't have written it. Be open to being wrong about the cause.

title: Technical Debt: Shortcuts Now, Pain Later
explanation: Technical debt is the cost of choosing an easy solution now over a better approach that takes longer. Like financial debt, it accrues interest: quick fixes make future changes harder and slower.
analogy: Like credit card debt. Buying now feels good. But interest adds up. Eventually, you're paying more in interest than on new purchases.
example: Copy-paste code instead of abstracting? Quick win. Now there are 10 copies. Bug found - fix it 10 times. Feature request - update 10 places. Debt paid with interest.
why_it_matters: Some debt is strategic (ship faster now). But unmanaged debt slows teams to a crawl. Recognize when you're taking debt; pay it down.
checkpoint_question: When is technical debt acceptable?
expected_answer: When speed matters more than perfection - MVP, experiment, deadline. Key: know you're taking debt, document it, plan to pay it back. Accidental debt is worse than deliberate debt.
common_mistake: Never paying debt. 'We'll fix it later' becomes never. Schedule time for cleanup. Make debt visible - track it like bugs.
key_insight: If adding a feature takes 10x longer than it should, that's debt interest. The 'fix' is paying down debt, not working harder.

title: Feature Flags: Ship Without Shipping
explanation: Feature flags let you deploy code that's not yet active. Hide features behind if-statements you control. Turn features on for specific users, test in production, and roll back instantly without deploying.
analogy: Like a light switch for code. The wiring is installed (deployed), but the light is off (disabled). Flip the switch when ready.
example: Deploy new checkout flow behind flag. Enable for 1% of users. Monitor. Increase to 10%, 50%, 100%. If bugs, flip flag off immediately.
why_it_matters: Decouple deployment from release. Deploy anytime, release when ready. Instant rollback without redeploy. A/B test easily.
checkpoint_question: Why enable a feature for only some users first?
expected_answer: Gradual rollout limits blast radius. If the feature has bugs, only 1% see them. Fix before expanding. Also enables A/B testing: compare old vs new.
common_mistake: Leaving old flags forever. Dead flags become confusing cruft. Remove flags after feature is fully released and stable.
key_insight: Feature flags enable trunk-based development. Everyone commits to main. Features hidden until ready. No long-lived branches.
